fatal_errors: The falsification experiment compares processing routes but cannot distinguish grain-boundary strengthening from simple solid-solution strengthening.
The alloy composition and quantitative milling/SPS process window are unspecified.

The cited evidence does not directly establish nanocrystalline dual-phase formation by mechanical alloying plus SPS without intermetallics; E2 and E3 instead attribute strengthening partly to a Laves intermetallic.
explanation: The hypothesis recovers the central processing concept—mechanical alloying followed by spark plasma sintering—and the intended sub-50 nm dual-solid-solution microstructure. It also broadly identifies grain refinement and solid-solution strengthening. However, it omits the equimolar CoCrFeNiTi powder system, milling time, speed, atmosphere, ball-to-powder ratio, and the 900–1000°C SPS window. It does not reconstruct the 83% FCC/17% BCC constitution, dislocation-density contribution, Ti-dependent phase stabilization, densification, or quantitative hardness and strength outcomes. Its boundary merely restates failure criteria rather than identifying thermal coarsening or phase-decomposition limits. Most importantly, comparison with cast material confounds porosity, grain size, phase constitution, and chemistry, so it cannot isolate Hall–Petch strengthening from solid-solution strengthening. A discriminating test would hold composition, density, and phase fractions constant while systematically annealing to vary grain size, then test whether yield strength follows a Hall–Petch relation alongside XRD/TEM measurements of grain size and dislocation density.
